steps.label: Conclusion (should)
steps.body: If the medical establishment wants people to pay attention to health warnings, it should announce only conclusive results from definitive studies.

steps.label: Evidence (after all)
steps.body:
We're constantly bombarded by warnings about certain foods having adverse effects, based on initial studies' tentative conclusions.
People who are constantly subjected to fire drills eventually come to ignore the fire alarm.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On a Role question, find the conclusion first, then ask what the named claim does for it.

The conclusion carries the opinion word: the medical establishment should "announce only conclusive results". The next sentence opens with "After all," and that phrase hands us a reason for the claim right before it. So the fire drill sentence is support for the conclusion.

Now look at what kind of support it is. Fire drills have nothing to do with food studies. The physician pulls in a situation from a different area of life because it works the same way: people hear a signal over and over, the signal rarely means anything, and they stop reacting. Constant tentative warnings are the fire drills. A health warning that finally matters is the real alarm. That is an analogy.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
We're asked about the last sentence. Prediction: it's an analogy offered as support for the main conclusion, the claim that the medical establishment should announce only conclusive results.

Any answer that calls it an example of the health warnings themselves, an objection, or decoration is out before we read the details.

notes.body: An example would be one of the actual warnings the conclusion is about, such as a scare over a particular food. Fire drills aren't health warnings at all. The physician isn't listing a warning; the physician is comparing a different situation that works the same way.

"After all" tells us the fire drill sentence is a reason for the conclusion, so it can't play "no logical role". The physician also never questions the medical establishment's motives. The complaint is about the strategy of announcing tentative results, not about why the establishment does it.

This matches the prediction in both parts. "After all" makes the sentence support for the claim before it, which is the conclusion. And because fire drills come from a different area of life but follow the same pattern (repeated signals, little real danger, people tune out), the support works as an analogy.

The move for the next Role question: first decide support, conclusion, or opposing view using the indicator words. Then check the description of the claim. Here both halves of the answer had to hold, and they do.

An objection would have to make the conclusion less likely, and there's no opposing view anywhere in this argument. The fire drill line pushes the same way the physician does: it explains why constant warnings backfire, which is exactly why the physician wants fewer, conclusive ones.

The physician does mention tentative conclusions and definitive studies, but the fire drill line doesn't explain how those two differ. Remove it and the difference between a tentative result and a conclusive one is just as clear. Its job is to show what too many warnings do to people.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (should)
old_steps.body: If the medical establishment wants people to pay attention to health warnings, it should announce only conclusive results from definitive studies.

old_steps.label: Evidence (after all)
old_steps.body:
We're constantly bombarded by warnings about certain foods having adverse effects, based on initial studies' tentative conclusions.
People who are constantly subjected to fire drills eventually come to ignore the fire alarm.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The main conclusion should be an Author's Opinion and it should be supported by at least one claim. We can find our conclusion here by noticing the Opinion Indicator should in the 2nd sentence, and by noticing the Support Indicator after all beginning the 3rd sentence.
"After all" is the "A" in FABS: for, after all, because, since
Whenever we see "after all", we know the previous claim was a conclusion.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We're being asked about the last claim, which we know was Support (the "after all" guarantees that). And we know the conclusion was the 2nd sentence.

old_notes.body: This answer treats the fire alarm as a literal instance of the type of warning the physician is concerned about — as if the physician were compiling a list of warnings that cause desensitization. But the physician is not cataloging types of warnings. The fire alarm is brought in from a completely different domain (building safety, not health research) to serve as an analogy. Its function is to illustrate a principle — that repeated alerts lead to desensitization — not to exemplify the specific health warnings under discussion. An example would be: "People hear about a different food causing cancer every week." An analogy is: "It is like fire drills — repeat them enough and people stop reacting." The physician is doing the latter, using a familiar non-health scenario to illuminate the dynamics of the health-warning problem.

Claiming a statement "plays no logical role" means it is tangential, decorative, or irrelevant to the argument's structure. That description is plainly false here. The fire alarm analogy is one of the physician's primary tools for supporting the conclusion. It is introduced with "After all," which is a premise indicator signaling that what follows provides a reason to believe what came before. Remove the analogy and the argument loses a key piece of its persuasive architecture. Additionally, this answer suggests the statement is meant to impugn the motives of researchers, but the physician is not questioning researchers' motives at all — the physician is arguing about the practical consequences of how research findings are communicated. The fire alarm analogy addresses desensitization effects, not researchers' intentions.

The fire alarm statement functions as an analogy that supports the physician's overall conclusion. The physician's main claim is that researchers should announce only conclusive results because excessive warnings cause desensitization. The fire alarm reference illustrates this desensitization principle through a parallel from everyday life: people subjected to repeated fire drills eventually ignore the alarm, just as people bombarded with constant health warnings eventually tune them out. The word "After all" explicitly marks this as a premise — evidence offered in support of what preceded it. The analogy does not form the conclusion itself; it supports the conclusion by providing a familiar, intuitive case that demonstrates the underlying mechanism (repeated alerts leading to diminished response). Its role is to make the abstract principle of desensitization concrete and persuasive.

This answer gets the relationship between the analogy and the conclusion exactly backwards. An analogy that "forms part of an objection to the conclusion" would be deployed by an opponent to undermine the physician's reasoning. But the fire alarm analogy comes from the physician and is offered in direct support of the physician's own conclusion. The relationship between the analogy and the conclusion is cooperative, not adversarial. The physician introduces the fire alarm to make the case for limiting announcements stronger, not to raise doubts about it. If the analogy were being used against the physician's position, it would need to highlight why desensitization does not occur or why frequent warnings are beneficial despite their frequency. Instead, it does precisely the opposite.

Clarifying a distinction means separating two concepts that might be confused — demonstrating how they differ from each other. The fire alarm analogy does the opposite: it highlights a similarity between two scenarios, not a difference. The physician's rhetorical strategy depends on the audience seeing fire alarm desensitization and health warning desensitization as parallel phenomena, not as distinct ones. Furthermore, this answer specifies a distinction between "initial findings" and "definitive study results," but the fire alarm analogy does not map onto that distinction. The analogy illustrates the consequence of overexposure to warnings in general, not the difference between preliminary and conclusive research. The analogy's function is comparison, not differentiation.

steps.label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
steps.body: Producing characters more automatically frees up mental resources for other activities.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Among 100 first-graders who got handwriting lessons, those whose composition skills had improved the most were the ones who had learned to write letters the most automatically.

Notice the mismatch: the composition half is about improvement, while the handwriting half is about how automatic the kids ended up.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a study that hands us a correlation, and the author reads a cause into it.

CURIOUS FACT: Why were the kids with the biggest composition gains the same kids who wrote letters most automatically?

AUTHOR'S EXPLANATION: Handwriting lessons made writing automatic for some kids. Once forming letters stopped taking effort, those kids had attention left over for what they were writing, so their composition improved.

Now argue with it. How could we explain the same data without the author's story? Maybe some kids were simply stronger students from the start. They could already write letters automatically before the lessons, and they also picked up composition faster, with no help from automatic handwriting. The evidence doesn't rule that out, because it never tells us whether automaticity changed during the lessons.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Strengthen answers for a curious fact usually do one of two things: make the author's explanation more plausible, or rule out an alternate explanation.

The best target here: show that the kids who gained the most automaticity during the lessons also gained the most in composition. Change tracking change is what we'd expect if automatic handwriting frees up attention, and it shrinks the room for the stronger-students-from-the-start story.

notes.body: This connects practice to automatic handwriting. That just tells us how kids became automatic. Composition never appears, so it does nothing to show that automatic writing frees up mental resources for other activities.

This one tempts because it links automatic writing with composition gains. But it is about kids who were already automatic before the lessons, and that fits both stories equally well: automatic writers had attention free, or they were simply stronger students who would improve at composition anyway. An answer that fits the rival as well as the author's story can't favor the author. B never shows that becoming more automatic did anything.

This is the prediction. The evidence only said the best improvers ended up most automatic. C says the kids whose automaticity improved more also generally improved more at composition. Now the gain in one skill tracks the gain in the other during the same lessons, which is what the author's story predicts and what the stronger-students story doesn't need.

The move: when a study's evidence compares a starting trait with an improvement, look for an answer that turns it into change matching change.

A representative group helps us apply the results to first-graders in general. It doesn't touch the real question, which is whether automatic handwriting causes the composition gains or something else explains both.

This runs the other way. Kids who started with strong composition skills became much more automatic, which hints that composition skill (or general ability) drives automaticity. That's a rival story, not support for the author's one.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
old_steps.body: Producing characters more automatically frees up mental resources for other activities.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Among first-graders who got handwriting lessons, those whose composition skills improved most were those who had learned to write letters most automatically.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The most common argument pattern on Str / Wkn is Explain Curious Fact, and when we see we're dealing with an Experiment / Study, we're almost always going to hear about some data from the study which creates the causal mystery that our author wants to solve.
CURIOUS FACT How come the kids whose composition skills had improved the most were the same as the kids who had learned to write letters most automatically? (you'd never guess this, but the LSAT author is about to assume that this correlation proves causation)
EXPLANATION We gave them handwriting lessons; they learned to write letters automatically. Once their handwriting became automatic muscle memory, that freed up mental resources for them to focus on what they were writing about / how they were communicating their ideas. So their composition skills improved. Notice how much I fleshed out the causal story being implied by the conclusion. Causal conclusions often suggest a longer story than they explicitly say, so we need to take a few secs to play out the author's causal chain in our brain.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body:
For Explain Curious Fact arguments, Strengthen questions usually **increase the plausibility** of the Author's Explanation, but sometimes they **rule out** an Alternate Explanation. So we want more evidence that becoming more automatic with your writing frees up cognitive bandwidth for you to focus on the quality of your composition.
Or we want to rule out some alternate explanation for why the kids with the biggest uptick in automaticity also had the biggest uptick in composition skills (f.e. the kids with the most automatic handwriting were **not** more likely to have English tutors they worked with outside of school).

old_notes.body: This links practice to automatic handwriting. Composition never comes into it, so it says nothing about freeing up mental resources.

This is about kids who were already automatic before the lessons. The argument is about becoming more automatic during them. Those kids might also just be stronger students overall, so this doesn't show automaticity freed anything up.
Across the group, bigger gains in automatic handwriting came with bigger gains in composition. That's the pattern you'd expect if automatic writing frees attention for composing.
A representative sample lets the result generalize. It doesn't support the causal claim about why automatic handwriting helps.
This suggests strong composition skills led to more automatic handwriting. That reverses the argument's direction of cause.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Medications with an unpleasant taste are generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form.
PT → (T or C or SG)

The active ingredient in medication M is a waxy substance that cannot tolerate the heat used to manufacture tablets because it has a low melting point.
~T

The company developing M does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology and manufactures all its medications itself.
~SG

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
M will most likely be produced in capsule form.
C

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion follows a process of elimination. Medications with an unpleasant taste are "generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form." M can't be a tablet, because its waxy ingredient can't take the heat. M can't be a soft-gel, because the company "does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology" and makes everything itself. Capsule is what's left.

But look at who the first rule covers: only medications with an unpleasant taste. Nothing tells us M tastes bad. If M tastes fine, the rule never applies, and M could come in a liquid, a powder, or anything else. The elimination only works if M is in the group the rule covers.
PT → (T or C or SG)
~T
~SG
missing: PT

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem says "if which one of the following is assumed", so we want the piece that makes the conclusion follow. The missing piece is the rule's trigger: M has an unpleasant taste. Once that's in place, the three-option rule applies, two options are gone, and capsule is the one left.

notes.body: If M can be made as a liquid, that adds a fourth option outside tablet, capsule, and soft-gel. That makes capsule less certain, not more. It also does nothing to show that M tastes unpleasant, so the three-option rule still isn't triggered.

This is the missing trigger. With M tasting unpleasant, the first premise applies: M will generally come as a tablet, capsule, or soft-gel. The heat rules out tablet, the company's missing technology rules out soft-gel, and capsule is what remains.
PT → (T or C or SG)
PT, ~T, ~SG, so C

The move: when an argument eliminates options from a rule, check that the rule actually applies to the thing in the conclusion.

This says a capsule medication isn't also a soft-gel (C → ~SG). We already know M won't be a soft-gel, so this adds nothing. And it still doesn't tell us M is limited to the three forms, because nothing says M tastes unpleasant.

If most low-melting-point medications are soft-gels, that points M toward a form this company can't make. It gives no reason to think M ends up as a capsule, and it never puts M under the unpleasant-taste rule.

This gives a reason to choose capsules for bad-tasting medicine, but it only matters if M tastes bad. E never says it does. Without that, M isn't covered by the rule and could be produced in a form outside the three listed.

old_steps.body:
Medications with an unpleasant taste are generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form.
PT → (T or C or SG)

The active ingredient in medication M is a waxy substance that cannot tolerate the heat used to manufacture tablets because it has a low melting point.
~T

The company developing M does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology and manufactures all its medications itself.
~SG

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body:
M will most likely be produced in capsule form.
C

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The argument assumes that medication M has an unpleasant taste.
PT

old_notes.body: Knowing M can be made as a liquid does not help the conclusion. If anything, it opens a fourth option besides tablet, capsule, and soft-gel. Only the premise about unpleasant-tasting medications limits M to those three forms, and that premise applies only if M tastes unpleasant.

This provides the missing assumption.
PT

This suggests that if a medication is produced in capsule form, then it is not produced in soft-gel form.
C → ~SG
Other medications are not relevant to this argument.

This reverses an inference from the evidence.
C → ~PT

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
In ancient Greek courts, witnesses were not cross-examined, and the jury, "selected from the citizenry," "received no guidance on points of law".
So it was extremely important for litigants to make a good impression on the jurors.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Courtroom oratory by litigants is a good source of data on the common conceptions of morality held by the citizens of ancient Greece.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence tells us litigants worked hard to impress jurors. The conclusion jumps to something else: that their speeches show what ordinary citizens thought was moral.

How could we argue against that? Maybe litigants impressed jurors some other way: with charm, flattery, appeals to class, or clever storytelling. Then the speeches would tell us what jurors found appealing, not what they believed about right and wrong. Maybe litigants presented an ideal moral code nobody actually held.

For the speeches to be a good record of common morality, two links have to hold. Litigants tried to impress jurors by appealing to the jurors' moral views. And the jurors' views were the citizens' views, which the argument already gives us since jurors came from the citizenry.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that connects impressing jurors to morality: litigants believed that sounding morally like the jurors was how to win them over. Then the speeches had to mirror the jurors' moral views, and those were the common views.

notes.body: Personality isn't morality. If jurors went by personality, the speeches would show what personalities jurors liked, not what citizens believed was moral. This connects impressing jurors to the wrong thing.

This says jurors scrutinized moral codes more closely than other people did. Close scrutiny doesn't tell us what jurors wanted to hear. Litigants might respond by presenting an idealized code instead of the common one, so the speeches still might not reflect ordinary moral views.

This is the link we predicted. If litigants believed jurors were impressed by a "professed moral code" that resembled their own, litigants would shape their speeches to echo the jurors' morals. Jurors were ordinary citizens, so the speeches would reflect common moral views.

The move: when the evidence is about one goal (impress jurors) and the conclusion is about something else (morality), look for the answer that ties the goal to the conclusion's subject.

If jurors favored litigants of their own economic class, litigants would pitch their speeches to class, not to shared moral views. The oratory would then show what appealed to the jurors' class, which points away from the conclusion.

The argument says jurors "received no guidance on points of law". If litigants still expected jurors to decide on a good understanding of the law, they would argue the law rather than appeal to morals. The speeches would then tell us less about common moral views.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: It was extremely important for litigants to make a good impression on the jurors.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Courtroom oratory by litigants is a good source of data on the common conceptions of morality held by the citizens of ancient Greece.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The argument assumes that impressing the jurors was best accomplished by reflecting the common conceptions of morality held by the citizenry.

old_notes.body: Personality isn't morality. If jurors went by personality, the speeches would show what personalities jurors liked, not what the citizens believed was moral.

Close scrutiny of one’s moral code does not necessarily mean that the moral code was going to reflect the average citizen. It could be that litigants would profess an idealized moral code rather than one that accurately reflected the average citizen.

If litigants thought jurors favored people whose professed morals matched their own, litigants would shape their speeches to the jurors' morals. Jurors were ordinary citizens, so the speeches would reflect common moral views.

If jurors favored litigants of their own economic class, litigants would pitch their speeches to class, not to shared moral views. The oratory would then show what appealed to the jurors' class, which weakens the claim that it reflects common conceptions of morality.

If litigants expected jurors to decide on a good understanding of the law, they would argue the law rather than appeal to the jurors' morals. The speeches would then tell us less about common moral views, so E weakens the argument.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The burrowing activities of sand termites cause fairy circles to form.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Sand termite colonies were found in every fairy circle the scientists investigated.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a correlation (termites are always there) turned into a cause (termites make the circles).

How else could we explain termites showing up in every circle? Maybe the arrow runs the other way: something else kills the grass, and termites move into the bare patches afterward. Or something else entirely, such as the soil or the climate, creates the circles, and termites just happen to live in the same ground.

So we want evidence that the circles form the way burrowing would make them form, or evidence that knocks out a rival cause.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Best target: something about how plants die in the circles that matches termites burrowing underground, especially while the circles are forming. Ruling out a rival such as termites arriving after the circles already exist would also work.

notes.body:
This matches the mechanism. Burrowing termites work underground, and here the grass dies from the roots only, with no damage above. It also describes newly forming circles, so the damage happens as the circle appears, which cuts against termites showing up afterward. It doesn't prove the hypothesis, but it makes the burrowing story fit the facts much better.

The move: when a hypothesis names a specific mechanism, look for evidence that the effect shows that mechanism's fingerprint.

This is about the grasses around the circles, not inside them. At most it suggests drought isn't what kills those grasses, which removes one rival. But it says nothing about what kills the plants that do die, and dropping one rival doesn't point to termites over every other cause.

Wetter soil inside the circles doesn't point to burrowing. It could just be an effect of the bare ground: no plants are drinking the water. It could even attract termites to circles that formed some other way, which is the reverse direction the argument needs to avoid.
Circles forming near other circles fits almost any local cause: the soil, the water table, or termites. Since it is equally consistent with every story, it doesn't make the termite story more likely.

Termite predators near the circles only confirms that termites live there, which the evidence already told us. Being present at the scene isn't the same as causing the circles, so this adds nothing to the causal claim.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Sand termite burrowing causes fairy circles to form.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Sand termite colonies were found in every investigated fairy circle.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The argument leans on a correlation. To strengthen, link the actual damage pattern to termite burrowing.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Pick the answer that shows fairy-circle damage is consistent with termite burrowing activity.

old_notes.body: Damage only at the roots fits termite burrowing — an underground cause matching the proposed mechanism.
Drought-resistant surrounding grasses cut against, not for, the termite hypothesis.
Higher water content does not specifically implicate termite burrowing as the cause.
Clustering is consistent with many causes; it does not specifically support termites.
Predators near circles only re-confirms termite presence; it does not show termite burrowing causes the circles.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In northern Europe, archaeologists have discovered 400,000-year-old sharpened wooden poles alongside flint cutting implements and the remains of horses. It is normally assumed that Homo sapiens did not inhabit Europe prior to 200,000 years ago.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: This discovery [the sharpened poles, cutting implements, and remains] effectively disproves the widespread belief that the humanlike precursors of Homo sapiens were entirely gatherers and scavengers and did not hunt.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with who made the poles. If Homo sapiens weren't in Europe until 200,000 years ago, then the 400,000-year-old poles belonged to the humanlike precursors. The argument needs that part, and it gets it from the second premise.

The weak part is what the poles were for. The conclusion says the find disproves the belief that the precursors were only "gatherers and scavengers and did not hunt." That only works if the poles and flint were used to hunt.

How could we argue they weren't? Maybe the sharpened poles were for fending off predators. Maybe the horses died on their own, and the precursors used the flint and poles to cut up and carry away the carcasses. Either way, the find fits a group of scavengers just fine.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that shows the poles were used for hunting, or one that rules out the non-hunting uses, such as defense or handling scavenged meat.

notes.body:
This rules out the two best scavenger stories. If the poles weren't for "self-defense" and weren't used to "cut or transport scavenged carcasses", hunting becomes the likeliest use for sharpened poles found next to horse remains. It doesn't prove the precursors hunted, but it closes the gap the argument left open.

The move: when the evidence is a set of objects and the conclusion is about what they were used for, strengthen by eliminating the other uses.

This says people in the area used stones and sticks as tools. The argument already assumes the precursors made the tools. The open question is what the tools were for, and B doesn't say anything about hunting.

C is about when Homo sapiens evolved, but the premise that matters is about when they lived in Europe, and evolving earlier doesn't put them in Europe earlier. If it did anything, it would open the possibility of Homo sapiens having made the poles, which hurts the argument. Either way, it says nothing about whether the poles were used to hunt.

Behavior that varied across ecosystems tells us nothing about what this group in northern Europe did. Divergent behavior could include hunting or not, so D gives us no reason to think these poles were hunting tools.

This is about Homo sapiens who already hunted, not about the precursors. Knowing that later hunters kept scavenging and gathering gives no evidence that the precursors hunted at all, which is what the conclusion needs.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: In northern Europe, archaeologists have discovered 400,000-year-old sharpened wooden poles alongside flint cutting implements and the remains of horses. It is normally assumed that Homo sapiens did not inhabit Europe prior to 200,000 years ago.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: This discovery [the sharpened poles, cutting implements, and remains] effectively disproves the widespread belief that the humanlike precursors of Homo sapiens were entirely gatherers and scavengers and did not hunt.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: If we accept the assumption about Homo sapiens (humans) in the second premise, then the sharpened wooden poles and flint cutting implements were probably not made by humans and were likely made by our humanlike ancestors. However, we don't know what the poles and cutting implements were used for. We can't be certain that they were used for hunting, so their existence doesn't necessarily prove or disprove anything.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: A correct answer might support the idea that the sharpened poles or cutting implements were used for hunting. It could also refute the alternative possibility that they were used for something other than hunting.

old_notes.body: This answer eliminates two major alternative explanations for the sharpened poles. If the poles were not used for self-defense or for cutting and transporting scavenged carcasses, then the remaining plausible use is hunting. By ruling out non-hunting purposes, this answer strengthens the inference that the poles were hunting weapons. Combined with the horse remains found alongside, the hunting interpretation becomes much more compelling. The argument needed help closing the gap between "found tools near dead animals" and "used tools to kill animals," and this answer does exactly that.

This answer establishes that humanlike inhabitants used stone and wooden tools more than 400,000 years ago. This makes it more plausible that the discovered artifacts were made by humanlike precursors rather than some other agent, which reinforces a premise. But the argument's weakness is not about who made the tools — it is about what the tools were used for. Knowing that precursors were capable of making tools does not tell us whether those tools were used for hunting, self-defense, or processing scavenged food. This answer supports the premise but does not strengthen the conclusion.

This answer says Homo sapiens evolved from precursors at least 200,000 years earlier than normally assumed. Even if modern humans evolved earlier, the argument's second premise states they "did not inhabit Europe" before 200,000 years ago — and evolving earlier does not necessarily mean inhabiting Europe earlier. This answer challenges the timeline of evolution, not the timeline of European habitation, which is the relevant premise. And even if it did affect the timeline, it would not help determine whether the tools were used for hunting.

This answer says that humanlike precursors developed "widely divergent patterns of behavior" in different ecosystems. This is too vague to strengthen the argument. "Widely divergent behavior" could include hunting, but it could also include many other activities — tool-making for non-hunting purposes, complex social behaviors, shelter construction, or entirely different survival strategies. Without specifying that hunting was among these behaviors, this answer has no clear bearing on the conclusion. It broadens the range of possible behaviors without narrowing down to the one the argument needs to establish.

This answer says that prehistoric Homo sapiens who hunted did not abandon scavenging and gathering. This is about Homo sapiens, not about the humanlike precursors the argument discusses. Even applying it to precursors, the fact that hunting and scavenging coexisted does not help establish that the precursors hunted in the first place. If anything, the coexistence of multiple food-acquisition strategies makes it harder to determine from artifacts alone whether a particular set of tools was used for hunting, scavenging, or gathering. This answer does not help resolve the ambiguity about tool use that weakens the argument.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Over the long run, apple orchards that use organic farming methods cost no more to run than, and are just as productive as, apple orchards using conventional methods. Organically grown apples tend to be better tasting.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Organic orchards are likely to be more profitable than conventional orchards in the long run.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Profit is what you take in minus what you spend. The evidence says organic and conventional orchards cost the same to run and produce the same amount. So the only difference left is taste, and the conclusion bets that better taste means more profit.

How could we argue against that? Maybe buyers don't care about taste. If people buy apples by price or by looks, better tasting apples sell no better and earn no more. Then equal costs and equal output mean equal profit.

The argument needs better taste to turn into more money: higher prices, more sales, or both.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that better taste brings in more revenue, for example that apple demand or apple prices depend on flavor.

notes.body: A recent rise in organic farming doesn't tell us why farms switched or whether taste earns anything. Ask the test question: does this connect taste to revenue? It doesn't, so it leaves the gap where it was.

This links short-run profit to long-run profit, but we know nothing about organic orchards' short-run profits. With no information to plug in, B can't move the conclusion. The gap is between taste and money, not between time periods.

This is the prediction. If demand for apples is "based primarily on flavor", better tasting organic apples will be in higher demand, which means more sales or better prices. With costs and output already equal, more revenue means more profit.

The move: when the evidence holds everything equal except one difference, the right strengthener shows that the one difference matters to the outcome in the conclusion.
If most people buy the apples with the "lowest price", taste isn't what drives sales. Then better tasting organic apples wouldn't earn more, which pushes against the argument rather than for it.

This gives conventional apples an advantage in appearance. If buyers care about looks, conventional orchards might sell more, which cuts against the conclusion. It certainly doesn't connect better taste to more profit.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Over the long run, apple orchards that use organic farming methods cost no more to run than, and are just as productive as, apple orchards using conventional methods. Organically grown apples tend to be better tasting.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Organic orchards are likely to be more profitable than conventional orchards in the long run.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: To reach this conclusion, we need to assume that an orchard which grows apples that taste better is guaranteed to be more profitable. `better tasting → more profitable`. This link is missing from the argument as it's written.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We're looking for an answer which makes this missing link more likely to be true. We want more evidence showing that better tasting apples are more profitable.

old_notes.body: An increased use of organic farming methods does not establish that organic orchards are more profitable. There could be many reasons for the trend — environmental concerns, government subsidies, consumer pressure — none of which necessarily connect to profitability. More importantly, this answer does nothing to strengthen the specific link the argument needs: that better-tasting apples generate more revenue. The argument's gap is between taste and profit, and an industry trend toward organic methods does not bridge that gap.

This answer introduces a relationship between short-term and long-term profitability. Even if orchards that are profitable in the short term tend to remain profitable in the long term, this does not help the argument. The argument never discusses short-term profitability, and we have no information about whether organic orchards are more profitable in the short term. Without that information, this answer has no clear connection to the argument's conclusion. The gap the argument needs to bridge is between taste and profit, not between short-term and long-term profitability.

This answer directly bridges the argument's gap. The argument establishes that organic and conventional orchards have equal costs and equal productivity, with the only difference being that organic apples taste better. The conclusion that organic orchards are more profitable requires an assumption that better taste leads to higher revenue. If demand for apples is primarily based on flavor, then better-tasting organic apples will generate more demand and therefore more revenue. With equal costs and higher revenue, organic orchards would indeed be more profitable. This answer provides exactly the missing link between taste and profit.

Price sensitivity among consumers does not help the argument. The argument does not provide any information about the price of organic versus conventional apples. If most people prefer the lowest price, organic orchards would need to price their apples competitively. But we do not know whether organic apples cost more, less, or the same as conventional apples at retail. This answer fails to connect to the taste-to-profit link that the argument requires. Even if organic apples were cheaper, this answer still would not explain why they are more profitable — lower prices could mean lower revenue per unit.

Consumer preferences about the appearance of apples are not directly relevant to the argument. The argument is about taste, not appearance. There might be some relationship between how an apple looks and how it tastes, but neither the argument nor this answer establishes that connection. Without knowing whether appearance influences purchasing decisions more than taste does, or whether appearance correlates with taste, this information does not clearly strengthen or weaken the link between the superior flavor of organic apples and higher profitability. If anything, by suggesting conventional apples look better, it might slightly weaken the argument — but that depends on assumptions not provided.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: Our study suggests that siblings of first-born children will tend to be more adventurous than will the first-borns.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
First-born children in the study consistently showed "less cognitive plasticity than did their siblings." Cognitive plasticity is the willingness to accept new ideas.
It is "reasonable to think" that people open to new ideas will be adventurous in other ways.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The study only measured one thing: openness to new ideas. The conclusion is about something else: being adventurous. The psychologist bridges the two with a premise that is just "reasonable to think".

How could we argue against it? Plenty of people are open to new ideas and still avoid risk in everything else. Being adventurous probably depends on many things, and openness to ideas might be a small part of it, or no part at all. If so, the study's result tells us nothing about who is more adventurous.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for evidence that people with more cognitive plasticity really are more adventurous, for example that openness to new ideas goes along with risk-taking. That turns the psychologist's guess into something with support.

notes.body: Creativity isn't adventurousness, and a few famous first-borns don't affect a claim about how first-borns tend to compare with their siblings. If anything, these are small counterexamples, so A can't help the argument.

A first-born has more younger siblings than anyone else in the family. So if "the more younger siblings one has" means more plasticity, first-borns should be the most plastic, the opposite of what the study found. B cuts against the evidence and says nothing about adventure.

This shores up the weak bridge. The psychologist only said it was reasonable to link openness with adventure. C says other studies found that cognitive plasticity goes with "willingness to take risks", and taking risks is a clear form of being adventurous. Now the study's finding about first-borns connects to the conclusion.

The move: when a premise is introduced as a hunch, the strengthener is often outside evidence that the hunch is true.

Knowing that "several industry leaders have older siblings" gives us a tiny, narrow sample, and we're never told how many first-borns lead companies too. Running a business also isn't shown to be adventurous. Nothing here connects openness to new ideas with adventure.

Participants described themselves as "more adaptable than other people." That's true of most of the group, first-borns included, so it doesn't separate first-borns from their siblings. And adaptable isn't the same as adventurous.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
old_steps.body: Our study suggests that siblings of first-born children will tend to be more adventurous than will the first-borns.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: First-born children consistently exhibit less cognitive plasticity than did their siblings. Cognitive plasticity is a willingness to accept new ideas. It's reasonable that those who are open to new ideas will be adventurous in other ways.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: We know from the study that siblings of first-born children exhibit more cognitive plasticity. And we have the author's idea that having more cognitive plasticity will be more adventurous in other ways. So does that prove that younger siblings will tend to be more adventurous? Not totally. Perhaps our capacity for being adventurous is comprised of many factors ... cognitive plasticity might just be one of them.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: It's hard to say how they'll strengthen this argument, but we can just look for more evidence that younger children (meaning "not the oldest" child) are more adventurous, or more evidence that cognitive plasticity is connected to being adventurous.

old_notes.body: The existence of creative first-born geniuses, if anything, undermines the argument's conclusion rather than supporting it. The argument claims first-borns are less cognitively plastic and therefore less adventurous. Examples of highly creative first-borns suggest that the cognitive plasticity findings may not generalize as broadly as the psychologist claims, or that cognitive plasticity and creative genius are not as tightly linked as assumed. Moreover, "some great creative geniuses" is anecdotal evidence that does not establish a general pattern. It provides isolated counterexamples to the study's findings without supporting the bridge between cognitive plasticity and adventurousness. This pushes against the argument rather than strengthening it.

This answer actually undermines the argument. If having more younger siblings increases cognitive plasticity, then the study's results could be confounded by family size rather than birth order per se. A first-born in a family of two might have only slightly less cognitive plasticity than their one sibling, while a first-born in a family of six would appear dramatically less plastic compared to siblings who benefit from having many younger peers. This suggests the relationship between birth order and cognitive plasticity is more nuanced than the psychologist presents, and the clean first-born-versus-sibling distinction may be an artifact of family size. Rather than strengthening the bridge to adventurousness, this answer complicates the underlying evidence.

The argument's weakest link is the bridge from cognitive plasticity (willingness to accept new ideas) to adventurousness (willingness to take risks in behavior). The psychologist stated this connection as merely "reasonable to think" — an assertion without evidence. This answer provides exactly that missing evidence. If other studies have independently demonstrated a correlation between cognitive plasticity and willingness to take risks, the bridge is no longer speculation; it is empirically supported. The strengthening works in two steps: first, the study shows siblings have more cognitive plasticity than first-borns; second, this answer confirms that cognitive plasticity correlates with risk-taking (a form of adventurousness). Together, these make the conclusion — that siblings tend to be more adventurous — substantially more credible. This is the only answer that directly supports the inferential gap between the measured trait and the predicted behavior.

A study of business executives showing that "several" industry leaders have older siblings is too limited and too narrow to meaningfully strengthen the argument. First, "several" is a vague, small number that does not establish a pattern. Second, business executives are a specific subset of the population, and leadership in business may not reflect adventurousness generally. Third, having older siblings makes someone a non-first-born, but the observation that some non-first-borns became leaders does not establish the cognitive plasticity-to-adventurousness link the argument needs. The evidence is anecdotal, narrowly drawn, and does not directly support the bridge between measured openness and predicted behavior. A few data points from one industry cannot carry the weight of a general behavioral conclusion.

How participants characterized themselves before the study began is irrelevant to whether cognitive plasticity actually correlates with adventurousness. Self-assessment of adaptability is not the same as measured cognitive plasticity, and people's beliefs about their own traits do not validate the bridge between openness-to-ideas and adventurous behavior. Moreover, the fact that most participants thought they were more adaptable than their siblings is a universal self-flattery bias that tells us nothing about actual behavior. The argument needs objective evidence linking cognitive plasticity to adventurousness; subjective self-assessments from participants provide neither the objectivity nor the specificity required.
